text: SQLite handles concurrent writes through a combination of file locking and transaction management to ensure data integrity. When multiple processes attempt to write to the same SQLite database file, SQLite uses a recursive mutex to serialize access, allowing only one writer at a time. This prevents data corruption but can lead to performance bottlenecks in high-concurrency environments. SQLite also supports journaling modes like WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) to improve write concurrency by allowing reads and writes to occur simultaneously, though writes are still serialized. The default behavior is to use a shared lock for reading and an exclusive lock for writing, which can limit scalability. For applications requiring higher concurrency, using the WAL mode or separating read and write operations across multiple database files can help mitigate performance issues while maintaining consistency.

source: PEP 380 (motivation section), public domain, https://peps.python.org/pep-0380/
text: A Python generator is a form of coroutine, but has the limitation that it can only yield to its immediate caller. This means that a piece of code containing a `yield` cannot be factored out and put into a separate function in the same way as other code. Performing such a factoring causes the called function to itself become a generator, and it is necessary to explicitly iterate over this second generator and re-yield any values that it produces.

source: PEP 342 (motivation section), public domain, https://peps.python.org/pep-0342/
text: Coroutines are a natural way of expressing many algorithms, such as simulations, games, asynchronous I/O, and other forms of event-driven programming or co-operative multitasking. Python's generator functions are almost coroutines -- but not quite -- in that they allow pausing execution to produce a value, but do not provide for values or exceptions to be passed in when execution resumes. They also do not allow execution to be paused within the `try` portion of `try/finally` blocks, and therefore make it difficult for an aborted coroutine to clean up after itself.

source: PEP 255 (motivation section), public domain, https://peps.python.org/pep-0255/
text: For example, `tokenize.py` in the standard library takes this approach: the caller must pass a *tokeneater* function to `tokenize()`, called whenever `tokenize()` finds the next token. This allows tokenize to be coded in a natural way, but programs calling tokenize are typically convoluted by the need to remember between callbacks which token(s) were seen last. The *tokeneater* function in `tabnanny.py` is a good example of that, maintaining a state machine in global variables, to remember across callbacks what it has already seen and what it hopes to see next. This was difficult to get working correctly, and is still difficult for people to understand. Unfortunately, that's typical of this approach.
